summary: Young children (ages 4-6) compare how much containers HOLD (capacity) using the language full / empty / half full / quarter full / more than / less than, and by POURING water or sand from one container to another. The core hurdle is conservation of liquid: children tend to judge amount by the height of the liquid or the size of the container rather than by what it actually holds. The reliable strategy is to pour into a common container (or pour one into the other) to test, repeatedly contrasting a tall-thin container with a short-wide one so that height stops being trusted.
misconceptions: Taller liquid level or taller container = more (height-vs-amount / conservation of liquid)
Wider or physically bigger container = more, judging the container not the contents
Thinks pouring the same water into a different-shaped container changes the amount
Guesses from appearance instead of pouring to test

activities.title: Pour the same water back and forth (conservation)
steps: Fill a tall thin glass with water and set an empty short wide bowl beside it, ready to pour the same water from one to the other.
Pour the water from the tall glass into the empty wide bowl and back again; notice the level is high in the glass and low in the bowl, even though it is the same water.

Predict first, then pour each of two mystery containers (secretly holding the same amount) into its own identical beaker and check: the levels come out about the same (small spills or drips can make a tiny difference).
Say aloud what happened: the tall one never had more, it just looked that way because the glass is thin.
Hit half-full and quarter-full targets by pouring until the water reaches a marked line (about half, about a quarter is fine at this age).
activities.insight: The same amount of water can look very different in differently-shaped containers; when the containers are different shapes, the height of the liquid (or the tallness of the container) does not by itself tell you the amount. To be sure, pour into identical containers, where comparing the levels is fair.

activities.title: Which holds more? Compare capacity by pouring into a common measure
steps: Take two containers that look different in size — e.g. a cup and a jug, or a wide-short container and a narrow-tall one.
Fill each and pour into matching identical bottles/beakers so you can compare fairly by what each holds.
Decide which holds more by looking at the common bottles, not at the original containers.
Try a deliberately tricky case: a narrow-tall container that actually holds MORE than a wide-short one.
activities.insight: Capacity is about how much a container holds, which you find by pouring and comparing in a common measure — not by how big or wide the container looks.

activities.title: Real water and sand play with the language
steps: At a water or sand tray, fill, empty and pour between real containers of different shapes and sizes.
Describe containers as full, empty, half full and quarter full as you fill them.
Compare two containers aloud using 'more than' and 'less than'.
Make a glass that is 'about half full' and another that is 'about quarter full'.
Solve a practical problem such as 'Which cup has more water?' by pouring to find out.
activities.insight: Capacity language and comparison are grounded in the practical, hands-on act of filling, emptying and pouring with real materials.

activities.title: Scored comparison and fill-level items (check, not discovery)
steps: From pictures of pour outcomes, choose which container holds more.
Match containers to the labels full, half full and empty.
Put a set of containers in order by how much they hold.
Explain, where asked, how you could check an answer by pouring.
activities.insight: Children can recognise and apply capacity and fill-level language and reason about which holds more from pour evidence.

checkQuestion: Set out a tall thin glass and a short wide glass holding the SAME amount of water (so the levels differ), a cup, a jug, and some empty identical beakers. Watch how the child decides: (1) 'Do these two glasses have the same amount of water, or does one have more? How could you find out?' (2) 'Pour this full cup into the jug — which holds more, the cup or the jug?' (3) 'Show me a glass that is about half full.'
checkAnswer: (1) Recognises you can't tell from the levels alone and pours into identical beakers (or one into the other) to compare — finding them equal. (2) Determines capacity by pouring (the jug holds more because the cupful doesn't fill it). (3) Identifies or makes a half-full glass. Uses full / half full / more / less correctly.
